opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on. The first is just a selection effect in how benchmarks get made. When people design a benchmark, they usually want it to be hard for current models but not impossibly hard, because a benchmark where everything scores zero isn't very informative and doesn't get adopted. So you end up targeting tasks that sit just beyond the frontier. And given how fast compute and algorithmic progress have been scaling, "just beyond the frontier" doesn't stay beyond it for very long. You're essentially placing the bar a year or two ahead of where things are, and then the field catches up on roughly that timescale.

The second thing is that benchmarks tend to measure fairly narrow, well-specified skills: problems with clean answers you can grade automatically. Those are exactly the kinds of tasks where you'd expect models to improve fastest, because they're the easiest to train on, whether directly, through synthetic data, or just because similar material is abundant on the internet. So there's a mismatch: the things that are easy to benchmark are also the things that are easy to make progress on. The harder stuff, like long-horizon agency, working in messy real-world environments, or coordinating over weeks on a project, is much harder to turn into a clean benchmark, so it's underrepresented.

And then there's some degree of contamination and optimization pressure. Once a benchmark becomes a headline number, labs have strong incentives to push on it, and some of the test distribution leaks into training data one way or another. That doesn't mean the progress is fake, but it does mean a benchmark score tends to overstate how general the underlying capability is.

So my overall view is that rapid saturation is a real signal of progress, but you shouldn't read it as "models can now do everything humans can do in this domain." The gap between benchmark performance and actual economic usefulness is still pretty large, and I think that gap is the more important thing to track if you care about when AI starts transforming the economy.

r001.rationale: The candidate says benchmark designers target tasks just beyond current models rather than impossibly hard ones, so they appear within reach and get adopted; rapid progress then catches up.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few things going on, and it's worth separating them because they point in different directions.

The first is just selection. Benchmarks are made by people, and people make benchmarks that are tractable to create and to score. That means you need questions with verifiable answers, you need them to be reasonably short, and you need to be able to produce a lot of them. Those constraints push you toward tasks that look like exams: multiple choice, short answer math problems, coding problems with unit tests. And it turns out that the kind of thing that's easy to grade is also pretty close to the kind of thing that's easy to train on. So you shouldn't be surprised when a benchmark that was built to be convenient gets solved quickly. The convenience is the vulnerability.

The second thing is that benchmark creators tend to calibrate difficulty against the models that exist when they make the benchmark. If the current frontier model gets ten percent, that feels like a good benchmark, there's a lot of headroom. But ten percent on a well-structured task often means the model is already most of the way there. The remaining difficulty is not a cliff, it's a slope, and a couple more scaling steps or some targeted RL gets you up it. People systematically underestimate how close "barely able to do it" is to "reliably able to do it" in this domain.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually the most important, is that saturation on a benchmark doesn't mean the underlying capability is saturated. It means the benchmark stopped measuring it. If you look at something like MATH or GPQA, models reaching ninety-plus percent didn't mean models became as good as the best human mathematicians or physicists. It meant that particular slice of what those people can do got covered. The things that are hard to put in a benchmark, long-horizon tasks, tasks where the goal is ambiguous, tasks where you have to operate in a messy environment over days or weeks and get feedback from the world, those are the things that remain hard, and they're hard to benchmark for the same reason they're hard to do. You can't easily compress them into a thirty-second evaluation.

So my honest read is that fast saturation tells you less about how fast AI is progressing than people assume. It tells you that we're good at building evaluations for the narrow stuff and bad at building evaluations for the broad stuff. If you want a better signal, you look at things like task length horizons, or at whether models are actually substituting for labor in real workflows, and the picture there is much more gradual than the benchmark headlines suggest.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark creators set difficulty relative to existing models and may mistake a low score for substantial headroom, even when models are already close to solving the task.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of reasons. One is simply that AI capabilities are improving quite quickly, so a benchmark that looks difficult when you design it might be much less difficult by the time people are actually using it.

But there’s also a selection effect. We tend to build benchmarks around tasks where we can specify the problem clearly and check the answer cheaply. Those are also tasks where it’s relatively easy to give models useful feedback and improve their performance. Once a benchmark becomes popular, people put effort into doing well on it, so progress there can be much faster than progress across the full range of things we care about.

And benchmarks usually have a ceiling. If a model gets 95 percent and the next model gets 99 percent, you’re running out of room to distinguish them, even though their capabilities on harder problems might be quite different. So saturation doesn’t necessarily mean that the underlying domain is solved. It can mean that we’ve exhausted the difficulty of that particular set of questions.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks often use clearly specified tasks with cheap checking and useful feedback, making progress easier. It does not say benchmarks are created only when solving them already appears within reach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of things going on. One is that AI capabilities really are improving quite quickly. But another is that benchmarks are usually designed to measure something that current systems are just starting to be able to do. So you create a benchmark where the best model gets, say, 30 or 40 percent, and that looks like there's a lot of room for improvement. But it doesn't necessarily represent a very large gap in underlying capability. A few generations of models later, you can be at 90 percent.

There's also a selection effect: once a benchmark becomes popular, people put effort into improving performance on it. That doesn't have to mean training on the test questions. It can mean choosing training data, or tuning the model, in ways that improve the particular skills the benchmark measures.

And a lot of benchmarks consist of relatively short, self-contained tasks with answers that are easy to check. That's useful for measurement, but it leaves out a lot of what makes real-world work difficult—figuring out what the task is, dealing with ambiguity, and reliably carrying out a long sequence of steps. So saturating a benchmark doesn't mean you've saturated the economically useful capabilities in that domain. It can just mean that you've run out of resolution on that particular test.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks are usually designed around abilities current systems are just starting to demonstrate, so apparent low scores may still be close to high performance. That conveys the criterion’s point that benchmarks are created when solving them is already within reach.
